stem:
A 35-year-old presents in established labour at 39 weeks. A urine culture at 18 weeks grew group B Streptococcus at 10⁴ CFU/mL; she completed oral treatment and a test-of-cure culture was negative. A vaginal–rectal GBS swab at 36 weeks was also negative. She is afebrile, has intact membranes and no penicillin allergy.

What should the admitting maternity doctor do for GBS prevention?

options.label: A
options.text: Omit prophylaxis, as the 36-week swab supersedes the earlier urine result
options.explanation: GBS bacteriuria at any count in this pregnancy marks heavy colonisation and is an indication for intrapartum prophylaxis; a later negative swab does not remove it.

options.label: B
options.text: Omit prophylaxis, since treatment and a clear test of cure eradicated GBS
options.explanation: Antenatal treatment does not eradicate genital-tract colonisation, which commonly recurs; a clear urine culture does not change the intrapartum indication.

options.label: C
options.text: Start prophylaxis only if membranes remain ruptured for 18 hours or more
options.explanation: Prolonged membrane rupture is a risk factor used when GBS status is unknown; her bacteriuria is already an indication.

options.label: D
options.text: Give oral amoxicillin in labour to cover residual urinary colonisation
options.explanation: Intrapartum prophylaxis requires intravenous antibiotics to reach adequate levels before birth; oral treatment is not effective.

options.label: E
options.text: Start intravenous benzylpenicillin now and continue it until birth
options.explanation: GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy is an indication for intravenous benzylpenicillin in labour, regardless of treatment or a later negative swab.

context: GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy warrants intrapartum prophylaxis even after treatment and a later negative swab.
